chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn Ahmad ibn A'sham, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari, from Hariz ibn Abdullah, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said:

He said: A child was born during the time of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) who had two heads and two chests in one back. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was asked: Is he inherited as one or two? He said: 'Leave him until he sleeps, then call to him. If both wake up together, he has one inheritance share. If one wakes up and the other remains asleep, then he is inherited as two.'
ai.seo_question: How is the inheritance share calculated for a person with two heads and chests in one body according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *al-istishab* (presumption of continuity) and the flexibility of legal personhood (*shakhs*) based on observable signs of consciousness rather than fixed anatomical structure. Imam Ali’s (AS) ruling highlights the dynamic nature of inheritance shares, where the distinction between one or two heirs is determined by the simultaneous or separate awakening of the heads, reflecting a sophisticated approach to biological ambiguity in fiqh.
